source.title: Normalization of Neural Networks using Analytic Variance Propagation

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares normalization methods using validation performance and concludes that the proposed method does not share batch normalization's generalization properties; the versions do not cover these normalization comparisons directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation performance for normalization methods and discusses overfitting. Most plotted values are not stated numerically in the text. It does not test random-label memorization, width scaling, convolutional versus fully connected generalization, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study compares normalization methods and initialization schemes. None of its results tests V1–V8: batch size is fixed at 128, Adam is used throughout, and architecture differs across datasets rather than being compared on the same task. Its normalization findings concern generalization but fit no supplied version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Analytic propagation normalization improves robustness to initialization and often lowers the training objective, while lacking BN's observed generalization advantage. BN is unstable from some alternative initializations. This does not mean AP2 cannot generalize: it matches BN on noisy MNIST.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares analytic propagation, batch, weight, and no normalization, with optimized learning rates and multiple initializations; it does not reproduce the interventions in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization comparisons vary with dataset and initialization; AP2 is on par with BN on noisy MNIST, while BN shows better validation performance on MNIST from BN initialization and a stated generalization boost in evaluation mode on noisy CIFAR-10.

fits_no_version.finding: BN gives better validation accuracy and less overfitting on translated MNIST; AP2 matches BN when Gaussian noise is added. On noisy CIFAR-10, the authors report an evaluation-mode generalization boost for BN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization methods can differ in held-out performance, with the differences depending on augmentation, initialization, and the statistics used at evaluation.

record.problems: Validation values are presented in plots without numerical values in the text. The paper notes that batch normalization evaluation performance on MNIST is stochastic and does not match training performance; the authors also state that their comparisons do not support conclusions about learning speed in noisy CIFAR-10.
record.rows_left_out: No plotted numeric points were reconstructed. Figure 3 reports training loss rather than generalization outcomes; Figures 5, 6, and 8 give validation outcomes described in the text and are represented by R1–R3.

untested.parts: Fitting fixed random labels and comparing held-out accuracy under natural and random labels.
Width scaling beyond the width required for zero training error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer performance and tuning-dependent differences.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout interventions, underfitting from excessive dropout, and removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8; the reported normalization findings themselves are supported by the supplied text. No additional result bearing on a supplied version was found.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local connectivity.
Large versus small batch training and recipe adaptations.
Dropout and its interaction with data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: simple non-convolutional network with 6 hidden layers of logistic transform units, 20 in each
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalization methods from BN initialization; validation performance reported for MNIST.

conditions.value: BN versus standard network, AP2, and weight normalization

rows.value: BN shows less overfitting and better validation accuracy.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison but gives no numerical validation values.
rows.check: Figure 5 supports the reported BN validation advantage, but normalization comparisons measure no supplied version. The MNIST condition includes random translations; it is not entirely unaugmented.

rows.operation_detail: Compared normalization methods from BN initialization; validation performance reported for noisy MNIST.
rows.value: AP2 is on par with BN.
rows.note: The text says overfitting does not occur in this task and describes AP2 as on par with BN.
rows.check: Figure 6 reports comparable AP2 and BN performance, not a partial instance of any supplied version. Conditions include random translations and added Gaussian noise.

rows.subject: CNN network with ReLU and specified convolutional layers
rows.operation_detail: Compared normalization methods; validation accuracy reported for noisy CIFAR-10.

conditions.value: BN in evaluation mode versus other methods

rows.value: BN has a significant generalization boost when using accumulated statistics (evaluation mode).
rows.note: The text calls this an interesting phenomenon and suggests a possible relation to boosting or ensemble techniques.
rows.check: The normalization result measures no supplied version. The cited discussion and Figure 8 cover all three initializations, not only init=None. The network uses leaky ReLU with slope 0.03 on negative inputs. The text attributes a boost to BN evaluation mode, but Figure 8 does not separately plot batch-mode validation accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
